title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
summary: An [[eigenvector|eigenvector]] of a [[matrix|matrix]] is a direction the matrix only stretches: $M\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$, where the number $\lambda$ is its [[eigenvalue|eigenvalue]]. When a $2 \times 2$ matrix has two different real eigenvalues, they turn any power $M^{n}$ into a formula in $n$. That is how you predict where a population moving between two towns ends up, years ahead.

goals.text: Test whether a vector is an eigenvector of a matrix, and find its eigenvalue.
Find the [[characteristic-polynomial|characteristic polynomial]] of a $2 \times 2$ matrix and solve it for the eigenvalues, by hand or with a GDC.
Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue of a $2 \times 2$ matrix.
Diagonalize a $2 \times 2$ matrix with two different real eigenvalues as $PDP^{-1}$.
Use $M^{n} = PD^{n}P^{-1}$ to find powers and long-term behaviour, and interpret them in context.

before.hint: For $\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ the [[determinant|determinant]] is $ad - bc$.
Each entry is a row of the matrix times the column vector.
before.explain: Row times column: $2(1) + 1(2) = 4$ and $3(1) + 4(2) = 11$. Multiplying the columns of the matrix by the vector instead gives $\begin{pmatrix}8\\ 9\end{pmatrix}$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.14}}.

before.hint: Factorise, use the quadratic formula, or use your GDC's [[polynomial|polynomial]] solver.
before.explain: $(x - 1)(x - 0.3) = 0$, so $x = 1$ or $x = 0.3$. Check: the roots add to $1.3$ and multiply to $0.3$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.8}}.

blocks.text: In {{lesson:1.14}} you multiplied a matrix by a column vector. Usually the result points in a new direction. For a few special vectors it stays on the same line: the matrix only stretches them.

Take $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Then $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, which has turned. But $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix} = 3\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$: the same direction, three times as long.

blocks.alt: Axes from 0 to 3. The vector v from the origin to (1, 1) and the vector Av from the origin to (3, 3) lie on the same dashed line y equals x, with Av three times as long as v. The vector w from the origin to (1, 0) and the vector Aw from the origin to (2, 1) point in different directions.
blocks.caption: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, $\boldsymbol{v}$ keeps its direction and is stretched by $3$. $\boldsymbol{w}$ is turned.

blocks.statement: Let $A$ be a square matrix. A non-zero vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ if $A\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$ for some number $\lambda$. The number $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue that goes with $\boldsymbol{v}$.
blocks.plain: An eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches, shrinks or flips. Its eigenvalue is the scale factor.

blocks.text: So $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $3$. Two facts follow from $A\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$.

1. Any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector, with the same eigenvalue. $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-5\\ -5\end{pmatrix}$ work just as well as $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$.

2. The zero vector never counts, even though $A\boldsymbol{0} = \lambda\boldsymbol{0}$ for every $\lambda$. An eigenvalue, though, can be $0$ or negative. A negative eigenvalue flips the vector to point the opposite way.
To test a vector, work out $A\boldsymbol{v}$ and see whether it is a multiple of $\boldsymbol{v}$.

blocks.question: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Show that $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A$, and find its eigenvalue. Is $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ an eigenvector of $A$?
steps: Multiply: $A\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}4(2) - 2(1)\\ 1(2) + 1(1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

Compare with $\boldsymbol{v}$: $\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix} = 3\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. So $A\boldsymbol{v} = 3\boldsymbol{v}$, and $\boldsymbol{v}$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $3$.
Test $\boldsymbol{w}$: $A\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}4 - 4\\ 1 + 2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

No single number times $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\end{pmatrix}$: the top entries need the multiplier $0$, the bottom ones $1.5$. So $\boldsymbol{w}$ is not an eigenvector.

blocks.question: Each year $6\%$ of the people living in Northby move to Southam, and $3\%$ of Southam's people move to Northby. No one else arrives or leaves. Let $x_n$ and $y_n$ be the populations, in thousands, after $n$ years. Then $\begin{pmatrix}x_{n+1}\\ y_{n+1}\end{pmatrix} = M\begin{pmatrix}x_n\\ y_n\end{pmatrix}$, where $M = \begin{pmatrix}0.94 & 0.03\\0.06 & 0.97\end{pmatrix}$. Show that $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $M$, find its eigenvalue, and interpret it.
steps: Read the matrix by columns: column 1 says where Northby's people go ($94\%$ stay, $6\%$ move). Column 2 does the same for Southam's.
$M\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0.94 + 0.06\\ 0.06 + 1.94\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
So $M\boldsymbol{v} = 1\boldsymbol{v}$: an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$.

Interpret: if the populations are in the ratio $1 : 2$, they stay exactly the same the next year, and every year after. The $6\%$ leaving the smaller Northby balances the $3\%$ leaving the larger Southam.

blocks.prompt: Which vector is an eigenvector of $\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$?
blocks.hint: Multiply each vector by the matrix. Is the result a multiple of the vector you started with?
blocks.explain: $\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$, so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $2$. The zero vector never counts. $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ goes to $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ to $\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}$: both have turned.

blocks.prompt: $\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $\begin{pmatrix}7 & -3\\2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Find its eigenvalue.
blocks.hint: Multiply, then compare the result with $\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: Guessing eigenvectors is slow. Find the eigenvalues first. Write $I$ for the $2 \times 2$ [[identity-matrix|identity matrix]], so that $\lambda\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda I\boldsymbol{v}$.

Then $A\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$ rearranges to $(A - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$. If $A - \lambda I$ had an inverse, multiplying by it would give $\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$. An eigenvector is never $\boldsymbol{0}$, so $A - \lambda I$ has no inverse: its determinant is $0$.

blocks.statement: A number $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of a square matrix $A$ exactly when $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.
blocks.why: $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ is exactly when $(A - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$ has a solution other than $\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$.

blocks.statement: For a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is $\det(A - \lambda I)$. It is a quadratic in $\lambda$, and its roots are the eigenvalues of $A$. The equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ is the characteristic equation.
blocks.plain: The quadratic you solve to find the eigenvalues.

blocks.text: Subtract $\lambda$ from each entry on the leading diagonal, then use $ad - bc$:

blocks.tex: \det\begin{pmatrix}a - \lambda & b\\ c & d - \lambda\end{pmatrix} = (a - \lambda)(d - \lambda) - bc = \lambda^{2} - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc)

blocks.text: This is not in the formula booklet, but it is quick to rebuild. A $2 \times 2$ matrix has at most two eigenvalues. You are only expected to find eigenvalues, by hand or with technology, for $2 \times 2$ matrices.

blocks.question: Find the characteristic polynomial of $A = \begin{pmatrix}6 & -2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Hence find the eigenvalues of $A$.
steps: Subtract $\lambda$ on the leading diagonal: $A - \lambda I = \begin{pmatrix}6 - \lambda & -2\\ 2 & 1 - \lambda\end{pmatrix}$.
Determinant: $(6 - \lambda)(1 - \lambda) - (-2)(2) = 6 - 7\lambda + \lambda^{2} + 4$.
So the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^{2} - 7\lambda + 10$. Check with the formula: $a + d = 7$ and $ad - bc = 6 + 4 = 10$.
Hence solve $\lambda^{2} - 7\lambda + 10 = 0$: $(\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5) = 0$, so the eigenvalues are $\lambda = 2$ and $\lambda = 5$.

blocks.text: Taking the diagonal entries, here $6$ and $1$, as the eigenvalues. That only works when an off-diagonal entry is $0$. Always solve $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.

blocks.question: A biologist splits a bird population into $j_n$ juveniles and $a_n$ adults, in hundreds, after $n$ years. Each year an adult raises $1.6$ juveniles on average, $30\%$ of juveniles become adults, and $70\%$ of adults survive. So $\begin{pmatrix}j_{n+1}\\ a_{n+1}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1.6\\ 0.3 & 0.7\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}j_n\\ a_n\end{pmatrix}$. Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of the matrix, to 3 s.f. Interpret the positive eigenvalue.
steps: Write down the equation you solve: $\det\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda & 1.6\\ 0.3 & 0.7 - \lambda\end{pmatrix} = 0$.
Expand: $(-\lambda)(0.7 - \lambda) - (1.6)(0.3) = \lambda^{2} - 0.7\lambda - 0.48 = 0$.
GDC polynomial solver with coefficients $1$, $-0.7$, $-0.48$: $\lambda = 1.126208\ldots$ or $\lambda = -0.426208\ldots$

Interpret: suppose the juveniles and adults are in the proportions of the eigenvector for $1.126\ldots$ Then each year the matrix multiplies both groups by $1.126\ldots$ The population grows by about $12.6\%$ a year and keeps those proportions.

blocks.text: Find the eigenvalues: write $\det(M - \lambda I) = 0$ and the quadratic before the values. That line earns the method mark, even when your GDC solves the quadratic.

blocks.hint: Expand $(7 - \lambda)(0 - \lambda) - (-4)(3)$ and set it equal to $0$.
blocks.explain: $\lambda^{2} - 7\lambda + 12 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda - 4) = 0$. The diagonal entries $7$ and $0$ are not the eigenvalues, because neither off-diagonal entry is $0$.

blocks.prompt: Use your GDC to find the larger eigenvalue of $\begin{pmatrix}0.5 & 0.8\\0.6 & 0.9\end{pmatrix}$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Use $\lambda^{2} - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc) = 0$. Here $ad - bc$ is negative.
blocks.explain: $a + d = 1.4$ and $ad - bc = 0.45 - 0.48 = -0.03$. Solving $\lambda^{2} - 1.4\lambda - 0.03 = 0$ gives $\lambda = 1.42111\ldots$ or $\lambda = -0.0211\ldots$

blocks.text: Once you have an eigenvalue $\lambda$, find an eigenvector by solving $(A - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}$.
1. Write out $A - \lambda I$ with the value of $\lambda$ put in.

2. Write the two equations from $(A - \lambda I)\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$. Because $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$, they say the same thing: one is a multiple of the other.
3. Use an equation that isn't $0 = 0$ to write $y$ in terms of $x$, or $x$ in terms of $y$. Give the free one a simple non-zero value, such as $x = 1$, or whatever makes both entries whole numbers.
4. Check that $A\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$.
If your two equations only allow $x = 0$ and $y = 0$, your eigenvalue is wrong. Recheck the characteristic equation: for a true eigenvalue they always share a non-zero solution.

blocks.question: $A = \begin{pmatrix}6 & -2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $2$ and $5$. Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
steps: $\lambda = 2$: $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2\\ 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, giving $4x - 2y = 0$ and $2x - y = 0$.
Both say $y = 2x$. Take $x = 1$: $\boldsymbol{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
$\lambda = 5$: $A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\ 2 & -4\end{pmatrix}$, giving $x - 2y = 0$, so $x = 2y$. Take $y = 1$: $\boldsymbol{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

Check: $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $A\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}10\\5\end{pmatrix} = 5\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.question: A bike-hire firm keeps $250$ bikes at two stations, A and B. Each day $20\%$ of the bikes at A end the day at B, and $30\%$ of those at B end at A. So the numbers at A and B are multiplied by $M = \begin{pmatrix}0.8 & 0.3\\0.2 & 0.7\end{pmatrix}$ each day. One eigenvalue of $M$ is $1$. Find an eigenvector for it. Hence find how many bikes should be at each station so that the numbers stay the same from day to day.
steps: $M - I = \begin{pmatrix}-0.2 & 0.3\\ 0.2 & -0.3\end{pmatrix}$, giving $-0.2x + 0.3y = 0$. The second equation is the same multiplied by $-1$.
So $0.2x = 0.3y$, or $2x = 3y$. Take $x = 3$, $y = 2$: $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
Every multiple $k\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ is also unchanged by $M$. The total must be $250$: $3k + 2k = 250$, so $k = 50$.
Interpret: with $150$ bikes at A and $100$ at B, the $30$ bikes leaving A each day exactly match the $30$ arriving from B. The numbers stay put.

blocks.text: You meet this balanced state again in {{lesson:4.19}}, as the steady state of a Markov chain.

blocks.prompt: $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $4$ and $-1$. Which is an eigenvector for $\lambda = 4$?
blocks.explain: $-3x + 3y = 0$ gives $y = x$, so $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Check: $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\4\end{pmatrix}$. $\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ is the eigenvector for $\lambda = -1$, not $4$.

blocks.prompt: A gym's members use morning or evening sessions. Each month $15\%$ of morning members switch to evenings and $45\%$ of evening members switch to mornings, so $M = \begin{pmatrix}0.85 & 0.45\\0.15 & 0.55\end{pmatrix}$. An eigenvector for the eigenvalue $1$ is $\begin{pmatrix}k\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. Find $k$.
blocks.hint: Use the first row of $(M - I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$.
blocks.explain: $(0.85 - 1)k + 0.45(1) = 0$, so $0.15k = 0.45$ and $k = 3$. Members split $3 : 1$ between mornings and evenings stay split that way.

blocks.text: A diagonal matrix has $0$s everywhere off the leading diagonal. Diagonal matrices are easy to work with: to multiply two of them, or to raise one to a power, you just work with the diagonal entries.
To diagonalize $A$, put its eigenvectors side by side as the columns of a matrix $P$. Put the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$, in the same order:

blocks.statement: If a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has two different real eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, with eigenvectors $\boldsymbol{v}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2$, then $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $P$ and $D$ as above.
blocks.why: Column by column, $AP = \begin{pmatrix}A\boldsymbol{v}_1 & A\boldsymbol{v}_2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1\boldsymbol{v}_1 & \lambda_2\boldsymbol{v}_2\end{pmatrix} = PD$. Eigenvectors of different eigenvalues are not parallel, so $\det P \neq 0$ and $P^{-1}$ exists. Multiply $AP = PD$ on the right by $P^{-1}$.

blocks.statement: [[diagonalization|Diagonalization]] writes a square matrix as $A = PDP^{-1}$. The columns of $P$ are eigenvectors of $A$, and $D$ is a diagonal matrix with the matching eigenvalues in the same order.
blocks.plain: Rewriting a matrix so that its eigenvalues do all the work.

blocks.text: You only diagonalize $2 \times 2$ matrices with two different real eigenvalues. $P$ is not unique: you may multiply either eigenvector by a non-zero number, or swap the columns. If you swap the columns of $P$, swap the eigenvalues in $D$ too.

blocks.question: Diagonalize $A = \begin{pmatrix}6 & -2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues and eigenvectors you found above. Check that $PDP^{-1} = A$.
steps: Eigenvalue $2$ goes with $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$, and eigenvalue $5$ with $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
Columns in that order: $P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $D = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & 5\end{pmatrix}$.
$\det P = 1 - 4 = -3$, so $P^{-1} = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

$PD = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 10\\4 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. Then $PDP^{-1} = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2 - 20 & -4 + 10\\4 - 10 & -8 + 5\end{pmatrix} = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}-18 & 6\\-6 & -3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}6 & -2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, which is $A$.

blocks.question: For the towns model $M = \begin{pmatrix}0.94 & 0.03\\0.06 & 0.97\end{pmatrix}$, find both eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each. Hence write $M = PDP^{-1}$, and interpret the second eigenvalue.
steps: $a + d = 1.91$ and $ad - bc = 0.9118 - 0.0018 = 0.91$, so the characteristic equation is $\lambda^{2} - 1.91\lambda + 0.91 = 0$.
Solve by factorising or with your GDC: $(\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 0.91) = 0$, so $\lambda = 1$ or $\lambda = 0.91$.

For $\lambda = 1$ you already have $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. For $\lambda = 0.91$: $M - 0.91I = \begin{pmatrix}0.03 & 0.03\\0.06 & 0.06\end{pmatrix}$, so $x + y = 0$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
So $P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ and $D = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 0.91\end{pmatrix}$.

Interpret: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ moves people from one town to the other with the total fixed. Each year $M$ multiplies that part of the populations by $0.91$. So any gap between the populations and the $1 : 2$ split shrinks by $9\%$ a year.

blocks.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\3 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $3$ with eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, and eigenvalue $-1$ with eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\end{pmatrix}$. You choose $P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\-3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Which $D$ gives $A = PDP^{-1}$?
blocks.hint: Which eigenvector is in the first column of $P$?
blocks.explain: The first column of $P$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, the eigenvector for $-1$, so $-1$ comes first in $D$. Then $3$ goes second, to match $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 4\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ is diagonalized as $PDP^{-1}$, with $\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\end{pmatrix}$ as the first column of $P$. Find the top-left entry of $D$.
blocks.hint: The top-left entry of $D$ is the eigenvalue of the first column of $P$. Work out $A\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: In a model $\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1} = M\boldsymbol{x}_n$, the state after $n$ steps is $\boldsymbol{x}_n = M^{n}\boldsymbol{x}_0$. A GDC finds $M^{10}$ for you. To see what happens for every $n$, or as $n$ grows, you need a formula for $M^{n}$.
Diagonalizing gives one. In $M^{2} = PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1}$, the middle $P^{-1}P$ is $I$, so $M^{2} = PD^{2}P^{-1}$. The same happens for every power:

This is in the formula booklet, with $P$ the matrix of eigenvectors and $D$ the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. $D^{n}$ is easy: raise each diagonal entry to the power $n$. Then multiply out the three matrices.

Long-term behaviour comes from the eigenvalues. As $n \to \infty$, $\lambda^{n} \to 0$ if $\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1$. If $\lambda = 1$, then $\lambda^{n} = 1$ for every $n$. If $\lvert\lambda\rvert > 1$, $\lambda^{n}$ grows in size without limit, changing sign each step when $\lambda < -1$.
Raising each entry of $M$ to the power $n$. That only works for a diagonal matrix, which is why you go through $D^{n}$.

blocks.question: For Northby and Southam, $M = PDP^{-1}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ and $D = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 0.91\end{pmatrix}$. Find $M^{n}$ in terms of $n$. The towns start with $50$ thousand and $40$ thousand people. Find the populations after $n$ years, and describe the long-term behaviour.
steps: $P^{-1} = \frac{1}{-3}\begin{pmatrix}-1 & -1\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$.
$PD^{n} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 0.91^{n}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.91^{n}\\2 & -0.91^{n}\end{pmatrix}$.

Populations: $M^{n}\begin{pmatrix}50\\40\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}90 + 60(0.91)^{n}\\ 180 - 60(0.91)^{n}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}30 + 20(0.91)^{n}\\ 60 - 20(0.91)^{n}\end{pmatrix}$ thousand.
Long term: $0.91^{n} \to 0$, so Northby tends to $30$ thousand people and Southam to $60$ thousand. The total stays $90$ thousand, split $1 : 2$ as in the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$.
Comment: the model assumes the same moving rates every year, with no births, deaths or other migration. That is unlikely to hold for decades, so the short-term figures are more reliable.

check.prompt: Now you try: find Northby's population after $10$ years, in thousands, to 3 s.f.
check.explain: $30 + 20(0.91)^{10} = 30 + 20(0.389416\ldots) = 37.788\ldots$, about $37\,800$ people. A GDC gives the same top entry for $M^{10}\begin{pmatrix}50\\40\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.alt: Graph of population in thousands against years n from 0 to 40. Northby starts at 50 and falls, levelling off towards a dashed line at 30. Southam starts at 40 and rises, levelling off towards a dashed line at 60.
blocks.caption: Northby, $30 + 20(0.91)^{n}$, and Southam, $60 - 20(0.91)^{n}$, settle at the $1 : 2$ split.

blocks.question: On an island there are $f_n$ foxes and $r_n$ rabbits, in hundreds, after $n$ years. A model is $\begin{pmatrix}f_{n+1}\\ r_{n+1}\end{pmatrix} = M\begin{pmatrix}f_n\\ r_n\end{pmatrix}$ with $M = \begin{pmatrix}0.6 & 0.5\\-0.2 & 1.3\end{pmatrix}$. At the start there are $300$ foxes and $600$ rabbits. Use $M^{n} = PD^{n}P^{-1}$ to find a formula for $f_n$. Find the number of foxes after $10$ years, in hundreds to 3 s.f., and describe the long-term behaviour.
steps: Read the model: with no rabbits, the foxes fall to $60\%$ each year. With no foxes, the rabbits grow by $30\%$. The $-0.2$ is rabbits eaten by foxes.
$a + d = 1.9$ and $ad - bc = 0.78 + 0.1 = 0.88$, so $\lambda^{2} - 1.9\lambda + 0.88 = 0$. Then $\lambda = 1.1$ or $\lambda = 0.8$.

$\lambda = 1.1$: $-0.5x + 0.5y = 0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. $\lambda = 0.8$: $-0.2x + 0.5y = 0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\end{pmatrix}$. So $P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 5\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, $D = \begin{pmatrix}1.1 & 0\\0 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$ and $P^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}-2 & 5\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$.

Start with $P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}-6 + 30\\ 3 - 6\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Then $\begin{pmatrix}f_n\\ r_n\end{pmatrix} = PD^{n}\begin{pmatrix}8\\-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}8(1.1)^{n} - 5(0.8)^{n}\\ 8(1.1)^{n} - 2(0.8)^{n}\end{pmatrix}$.
Long term: $0.8^{n} \to 0$, so $f_n$ and $r_n$ both get close to $8(1.1)^{n}$. Both populations grow by about $10\%$ a year, in the ratio $1 : 1$ of the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1.1$.
Comment: growth cannot go on for ever on an island with limited space and food, so the model only suits the short term.

blocks.text: Hence find $M^{n}$: write $M^{n} = PD^{n}P^{-1}$ with your own $P$, $D^{n}$ and $P^{-1}$ before you multiply. Check that your answer gives $I$ at $n = 0$ and $M$ at $n = 1$.

blocks.hint: For a diagonal matrix, cube each diagonal entry.
blocks.explain: $0.5^{3} = 0.125$ and $1^{3} = 1$. Multiplying by $3$ instead of cubing gives $1.5$ and $3$.

blocks.prompt: Deer move between two parks, X and Y. Each year the numbers in X and Y are multiplied by $M = \begin{pmatrix}0.76 & 0.16\\0.24 & 0.84\end{pmatrix}$. The eigenvalues are $1$ and $0.6$, with eigenvectors $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. There are $400$ deer in total. In the long term, how many deer are in park X?
blocks.hint: As $n \to \infty$, $0.6^{n} \to 0$. Only the part along $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ is left, and the total stays $400$.
blocks.explain: The deer end up split $2 : 3$, as in the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$. So park X has $\frac{2}{5} \times 400 = 160$ deer, and park Y has $240$.

blocks.text: For a square matrix $A$, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue with eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}$ when $A\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{v} \neq \boldsymbol{0}$. Any non-zero multiple of $\boldsymbol{v}$ is also an eigenvector for $\lambda$.

blocks.tex: \det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^{2} - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc) \quad \text{for } A = \begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}\text{; its roots are the eigenvalues}

blocks.text: To find an eigenvector for an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$, solve $(A - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$. The two equations are multiples of each other: pick any non-zero solution.
A $2 \times 2$ matrix with two different real eigenvalues can be written $A = PDP^{-1}$: eigenvectors as the columns of $P$, and the matching eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of $D$.

In $\boldsymbol{x}_n = M^{n}\boldsymbol{x}_0$ with $M = PDP^{-1}$, the part of $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ along each eigenvector is multiplied by its eigenvalue at every step. As $n \to \infty$ that part dies away if $\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1$ and stays the same if $\lambda = 1$. If it is not zero and $\lvert\lambda\rvert > 1$, it grows without limit.

mistakes: Putting the eigenvalues in $D$ in a different order from their eigenvectors in $P$. Column $k$ of $P$ must be the eigenvector of the $k$th diagonal entry of $D$.
Writing $M^{n} = P^{-1}D^{n}P$. With eigenvectors as the columns of $P$, it is $PD^{n}P^{-1}$: $P$ first, $P^{-1}$ last.
Giving the zero vector, or no vector, as an eigenvector. Choose a non-zero solution of $(A - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$ and check that $A\boldsymbol{v} = \lambda\boldsymbol{v}$.
Rounding an eigenvalue before raising it to a power. Small errors grow when the power is large, so keep the GDC's full value.
Stopping at $M^{n}$ or the eigenvalues when the question asks about the context. Say what happens to the quantities, with units, and comment on whether the model is realistic.
examTips: Describe the long-term behaviour: say which terms tend to $0$ because $\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1$, give the limiting values in context with units, and comment on whether the model stays realistic.
Find an eigenvector: any non-zero multiple of a correct eigenvector earns the marks, so choose whole numbers. Show the equation you get from $(M - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$.
Write down $D$: put the eigenvalues in the same order as their eigenvectors in the columns of $P$. If $P$ is given, first read which eigenvector is in each column.
Show that $\boldsymbol{v}$ is an eigenvector: work out $M\boldsymbol{v}$ and write it as $\lambda\boldsymbol{v}$. Work forwards from $M$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$; don't start from the answer.
